lines.text: Every app has a README full of promises. Add to cart. Sign up for the newsletter. But does the live app actually keep them?

sentences.text: Every app has a README full of promises.

lines.text: This is Greenlight. It checks every promise on your live app, using Kane CLI to test it, and Claude Code to fix what's broken.

sentences.text: This is Greenlight.

lines.text: You give it three things: your code on GitHub, the link to your live app, and your README. That's all. No account, no setup.

sentences.text: You give it three things: your code on GitHub, the link to your live app, and your README.

lines.text: Greenlight turns each promise into a claim it can test. You choose which ones to check, and you see exactly what the run will cost before anything starts. Nothing runs until you press Run.

lines.text: This is where Kane CLI comes in. Greenlight hands it every claim as a plain-English test. Kane opens your live app in a real browser and uses it the way a person would: it clicks, it types, it reads what's on the screen. The cart works. But the newsletter keeps saying no.

sentences.text: This is where Kane CLI comes in.

lines.text: And here is the verdict, claim by claim. The cart passed. The newsletter failed, and Kane tells you exactly what it saw. Greenlight doesn't stop at the problem. It brings up the fix, ready for Claude Code.

lines.text: First time using Claude Code? Greenlight walks you through it. Copy one line, and Claude Code is ready in a few minutes. You only do this once.

lines.text: Then click Connect Claude Code, copy one message, and paste it into Claude Code. That message is all it needs to find your check and talk to Greenlight.

lines.text: Claude Code reads Kane's verdict straight from Greenlight, including what Kane saw. It uses that to find the real cause: the form was misreading the server's reply. It fixes it, publishes the change, waits for the new version to go live, and asks Kane to check again. You just watch.
